questions.stem: What is an allele?
options: The pair of chromosomes that carries a particular gene
One of the alternative forms of a gene at a particular locus
The complete set of genetic material in the nucleus of an organism
The position that a gene occupies on a chromosome
questions.explanation: Alleles are different versions of the same gene, such as the alleles for blue and brown eye pigment, found at the same locus. The complete set of genetic material is the genome, and the position of a gene is its locus.

questions.stem: What is a genome?
options: The complete set of genetic material of an organism
The pair of alleles an individual has for one gene
The observable characteristics of an individual
A single chromosome carrying many linked genes
questions.explanation: A genome is all of an organism's DNA, including all of its genes. The pair of alleles for one gene is a genotype, and observable characteristics make up the phenotype.

questions.stem: Which statement describes a pair of homologous chromosomes?
options: They carry the same genes at the same loci, and one comes from each parent
They are identical copies of one chromosome made during S phase
They carry the same alleles at every one of their gene loci
They come from the same parent and pair up with each other during mitosis
questions.explanation: Homologous chromosomes match in size, centromere position and the genes they carry, but one is maternal and one paternal, so their alleles can differ. Identical copies made in S phase are sister chromatids. Homologues pair up in meiosis, not mitosis.

questions.stem: How many autosomes are in a normal human body cell?
questions.explanation: A human body cell has 46 chromosomes: 22 pairs of autosomes, which is 44, plus one pair of sex chromosomes. 22 and 23 are the counts in a sperm or egg, and 46 includes the sex chromosomes.

questions.stem: Body cells of a fruit fly have 8 chromosomes, a human 46, a potato 48 and a dog 78. What do these numbers show?
options: Chromosome number rises with body size, so larger species have more of them
Closely related species always have the same number of chromosomes
Chromosome number varies between species and is not a measure of complexity
Species with more chromosomes are always more complex than those with fewer
questions.explanation: Chromosome number differs widely between species, and a potato having more chromosomes than a human shows it does not track complexity. Fruit flies are smaller than potatoes and have fewer, but dogs, which are smaller than humans, have more, so number does not follow size either.

questions.stem: Chromosomes in a human karyotype are numbered 1 to 22 from largest to smallest. What makes chromosome 1 larger than chromosome 21?
options: It is a sex chromosome, so it carries extra genes for sex
It is present in more copies than chromosome 21 in each cell
It has been through more crossing over, which lengthens it
It contains a longer DNA molecule, with many more base pairs
questions.explanation: Chromosome size reflects the length of the DNA molecule it contains, so chromosome 1 carries far more base pairs, and more genes, than chromosome 21. Chromosomes 1 and 21 are both autosomes, each normally present as one pair.

questions.stem: What is a karyotype?
options: An image of a cell's chromosomes arranged in homologous pairs by size and shape
A diagram tracing an inherited trait through several generations of one family
A grid used to predict the genotypes of offspring from a genetic cross
A list of the base sequence of every gene found in a person's genome
questions.explanation: A karyotype is made by photographing chromosomes from a dividing cell, then arranging them in pairs by size, centromere position and banding. A diagram of a family is a pedigree, and a grid for predicting offspring is a Punnett square.

questions.stem: A karyotype shows 47 chromosomes, including three copies of chromosome 21 and two X chromosomes. What does this show?
options: A male with Klinefelter syndrome
A female with trisomy 21 (Down syndrome)
A male with trisomy 21 (Down syndrome)
A female with Turner syndrome
questions.explanation: Two X chromosomes and no Y indicate a female, and a third chromosome 21 is trisomy 21, the cause of Down syndrome. Turner syndrome is 45 chromosomes with a single X, and Klinefelter syndrome is a male with an extra X (XXY).

questions.stem: Why can a karyotype detect Down syndrome but not cystic fibrosis?
options: Down syndrome involves a missing sex chromosome, whereas cystic fibrosis is caused by an extra copy of an autosome
Down syndrome is caused by a dominant allele, which makes its chromosome visibly larger than normal
Cystic fibrosis affects the lungs, so its chromosomes are not present in the blood cells used
Down syndrome involves an extra whole chromosome, whereas cystic fibrosis is caused by a change in one gene
questions.explanation: A karyotype shows the number and broad structure of chromosomes, so an extra chromosome 21 is easy to see. Cystic fibrosis results from a change in the base sequence of one gene, which is far too small to see. Every body cell carries the full set of chromosomes, whatever tissue a disease affects.

questions.stem: What does meiosis produce from one diploid cell?
options: Four genetically identical haploid cells
Two genetically different haploid cells
Four genetically different haploid cells
Two genetically identical diploid cells
questions.explanation: Meiosis has two divisions, giving four cells, each with half the chromosome number. Crossing over and independent assortment make them genetically different. Two identical diploid cells are the product of mitosis.

questions.stem: When does crossing over occur, and between which structures?
options: In metaphase I, between chromosomes that are not homologous
In anaphase II, between chromatids moving to opposite poles
In prophase I, between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes
In prophase II, between the sister chromatids of a single chromosome
questions.explanation: Homologous chromosomes pair closely in prophase I, and non-sister chromatids swap matching segments at chiasmata. Exchanges between sister chromatids would change nothing, because they are identical copies.

questions.stem: What is independent assortment?
options: The random orientation of each homologous pair at the equator in metaphase I
The exchange of segments between non-sister chromatids in prophase I
The random fusion of any one sperm with any one egg at the moment of fertilisation
The separation of sister chromatids to opposite poles in anaphase II
questions.explanation: In metaphase I each homologous pair lines up independently of the others, so the maternal and paternal chromosomes are sorted into gametes in many combinations. Exchange of segments is crossing over, and random fusion at fertilisation is a separate source of variation.

questions.stem: An organism has a diploid number of 8. Ignoring crossing over, how many genetically different gametes can independent assortment produce?
questions.explanation: A diploid number of 8 means 4 homologous pairs, and each pair can orient two ways, giving 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 16 combinations. Using 8 pairs gives 256, which double counts, and 8 or 4 forget that the combinations multiply.

questions.stem: Which event in meiosis halves the chromosome number from diploid to haploid?
options: Separation of sister chromatids in meiosis II
Replication of DNA before meiosis begins
Crossing over between chromatids in prophase I
Separation of homologous chromosomes in meiosis I
questions.explanation: Meiosis I separates homologous pairs, so each daughter cell gets one chromosome from each pair: half the number. Meiosis II separates sister chromatids, like mitosis, so the chromosome number does not change again.

questions.stem: A human cell (2n = 46) has just completed meiosis I. How many chromosomes and chromatids are in each daughter cell?
options: 23 chromosomes and 46 chromatids
46 chromosomes and 92 chromatids
23 chromosomes and 23 chromatids
46 chromosomes and 46 chromatids
questions.explanation: Meiosis I separates homologous pairs, so each cell has 23 chromosomes, but each still has two sister chromatids, making 46 chromatids. Only after meiosis II, when the chromatids separate, does each cell have 23 single-chromatid chromosomes.

questions.stem: How does crossing over increase genetic diversity?
options: It creates new alleles by changing the DNA base sequence
It doubles the number of chromosomes in each gamete
It makes every gamete identical to the parent cell
It creates new combinations of alleles on the chromatids
questions.explanation: Swapping segments between maternal and paternal chromatids puts alleles together in combinations not found in either parent's chromosomes. It shuffles existing alleles rather than creating new ones; new alleles arise by mutation.

questions.stem: In pea plants the allele for tall stems (T) is dominant to the allele for short stems (t). What is the genotype of a short plant?
options: Heterozygous, Tt
Homozygous dominant, TT
Hemizygous recessive, t only
Homozygous recessive, tt
questions.explanation: A recessive phenotype appears only when both alleles are recessive, so a short plant must be tt. Tt and TT both contain a dominant T allele and would be tall.

questions.stem: What is a heterozygous genotype?
options: Only one allele at a locus, as for a male's XB Y
Two different alleles at a gene locus, such as Bb
Two identical dominant alleles at a locus, such as BB
Two identical recessive alleles at a locus, such as bb
questions.explanation: Heterozygous means the two alleles at a locus differ. BB and bb are homozygous, dominant and recessive. A male has only one X-linked allele, which is called hemizygous.

questions.stem: A red bull (CR CR) is crossed with a white cow (CW CW). All the calves are roan: their coat is a mixture of separate red hairs and white hairs. What inheritance pattern is shown?
options: Sex-linked inheritance
Codominance
Incomplete dominance
Complete dominance
questions.explanation: Both alleles are fully expressed side by side, as red hairs and white hairs, which is codominance. Incomplete dominance would give one blended, intermediate colour on every hair. Complete dominance would make the calves look like one parent.

questions.stem: Red snapdragons crossed with white snapdragons give all pink offspring. What phenotype ratio is expected if two pink plants are crossed?
options: 3 red : 1 white
1 red : 2 pink : 1 white
3 pink : 1 white
All pink
questions.explanation: Pink is the intermediate heterozygote of incomplete dominance. Crossing two heterozygotes gives 1 homozygous red : 2 heterozygous pink : 1 homozygous white, and because each genotype looks different the phenotype ratio matches the genotype ratio. A 3:1 ratio would need one allele to be dominant.

questions.stem: People with blood group AB have red cells carrying both A and B antigens. What does this show about the A and B alleles?
options: They are codominant
They show incomplete dominance
They are both recessive
They are X-linked
questions.explanation: In blood group AB both alleles are fully expressed, producing both antigens, which is codominance. Incomplete dominance would produce a single intermediate antigen. The A and B alleles are dominant to the O allele, and the ABO gene is on an autosome.

questions.stem: A man with blood group A (IA i) and a woman with blood group B (IB i) have a child. What is the probability the child has blood group O?
questions.explanation: Each parent passes on the i allele with probability 1/2, so the chance of an ii child is 1/2 × 1/2 = 1/4. The cross can give all four blood groups, A, B, AB and O, each with probability 1/4. Answering 0 assumes parents with groups A and B cannot carry the O allele.

questions.stem: Hydrangeas with the same genotype grow blue flowers in acidic soil and pink flowers in alkaline soil. What does this show?
options: Flower colour in hydrangeas is controlled by codominant alleles
Flower colour in hydrangeas is controlled by the plant's genotype alone, not its soil
The environment can influence how a genotype is expressed as a phenotype
Soil pH changes the alleles the plant carries for flower colour
questions.explanation: The plants share a genotype but differ in phenotype, so a factor in the environment, soil pH, must affect how the genes are expressed. The soil does not change the DNA, and codominance is a relationship between two alleles, which this comparison does not test.

questions.stem: Himalayan rabbits are white with dark ears, feet and tail. If fur on the back is shaved and the skin kept cold, the fur grows back dark. What explains this?
options: The enzyme that makes dark pigment is only active at lower temperatures
The cold causes a mutation in the fur-colour gene of the skin cells
The cold kills the cells that make white fur, leaving the dark cells
Shaving removes the allele for white fur from that patch of skin
questions.explanation: The rabbit's pigment enzyme is temperature-sensitive, so it works only in cooler parts of the body such as the extremities. Keeping the back cold lets it work there too. The genotype is unchanged; the environment alters how it is expressed.

questions.stem: Height in humans varies continuously across a population. Which explanation best fits this pattern?
options: A single gene with two codominant alleles controls it, giving three heights
Environmental factors alone control it, so it is not inherited at all
Many genes contribute, and environmental factors such as nutrition also play a part
A single gene with two alleles, one of them completely dominant to the other, controls it
questions.explanation: Continuous variation is typical of polygenic traits, where many genes each add a small effect, and environment shifts the result further. A single gene with two alleles gives two or three distinct classes, not a continuous range.

questions.stem: What is an epigenetic change?
options: A change in the number of chromosomes in a cell
A change in which alleles a child inherits from one of its two parents
A change in gene expression with no change in the DNA base sequence
A change in the base sequence of the DNA of a gene
questions.explanation: Epigenetic changes, such as DNA methylation and changes to histone proteins, alter whether genes are switched on or off without changing the DNA sequence. A change in base sequence is a mutation.

questions.stem: How does DNA methylation near a gene usually affect it?
options: It adds new bases, lengthening the gene
It moves the gene to another chromosome
It silences the gene, reducing its expression
It changes the order of bases in the gene
questions.explanation: Methyl groups added to DNA near a gene usually stop it being transcribed, so the gene is switched off. Methylation is an epigenetic mark: it sits on the DNA without changing its base sequence.

questions.stem: Identical twins have the same DNA sequence, yet at sixty one twin develops a disease the other does not. Which explanation is best supported?
options: When the embryo split, one twin received one more chromosome than the other twin received
Different environments over their lives led to different epigenetic marks, changing gene expression
One twin inherited different alleles from their mother at fertilisation than the other twin did
Their genotypes must have differed from birth, because epigenetic marks cannot change after birth
questions.explanation: Identical twins come from one zygote, so they inherit the same alleles. Epigenetic marks build up differently with diet, stress, smoking and other exposures, so gene expression can diverge as twins age. Epigenetic marks can change throughout life, which is why twins become more different over time.

questions.stem: In a pedigree chart, what does a shaded square represent?
options: A female who shows the trait
A male who is a carrier
A female who is a carrier
A male who shows the trait
questions.explanation: Squares represent males and circles females, and shading shows that the person has the trait. Carriers, where marked, are usually shown half-shaded or with a dot.

questions.stem: In a pedigree, two unaffected parents have an affected daughter. Which mode of inheritance does this show?
options: X-linked recessive
X-linked dominant
Autosomal recessive
Autosomal dominant
questions.explanation: An affected child of unaffected parents means the trait is recessive. It cannot be X-linked recessive, because the daughter would need a recessive allele from her father, and a father with it would be affected. Any dominant pattern needs at least one affected parent.

questions.stem: In a pedigree, two affected parents have an unaffected child. What does this show?
options: The trait is X-linked recessive, and the father is a carrier
The trait is recessive, and the child is homozygous recessive
The trait is dominant, and both parents are heterozygous
The trait is recessive, and both parents are carriers
questions.explanation: Affected parents can only have an unaffected child if each carries a hidden recessive allele, so the trait itself must be dominant and the parents heterozygous. If the trait were recessive, two affected parents would be homozygous recessive and every child would be affected. Males cannot be carriers of X-linked traits.

questions.stem: Which observation in a pedigree rules out X-linked recessive inheritance?
options: Unaffected parents have an affected son
An affected woman has an unaffected son
An affected man has unaffected daughters
More males than females are affected
questions.explanation: An affected woman has two recessive alleles, and every son gets one of her X chromosomes, so all her sons must be affected. An affected man's daughters are carriers, often unaffected, and a carrier mother can have an affected son, so those observations fit X-linked recessive inheritance.

questions.stem: An affected father and unaffected mother have four daughters and three sons. All four daughters are affected and none of the sons are. Which mode of inheritance is most likely?
options: X-linked dominant
X-linked recessive
Autosomal recessive
Y-linked
questions.explanation: A father passes his X chromosome to every daughter and none of his sons, so an X-linked dominant allele makes all daughters affected and no sons. X-linked recessive would leave daughters of an unaffected mother as unaffected carriers. A Y-linked trait would appear in sons, not daughters.

questions.stem: A woman who is a carrier of haemophilia (XH Xh) has children with an unaffected man (XH Y). What proportion of their sons are expected to have haemophilia?
options: All
One half
One quarter
None
questions.explanation: Every son receives his father's Y and one of his mother's X chromosomes, which is Xh half the time. So half the sons are expected to be affected. One quarter is the chance that any child is an affected son, which is a different question.

questions.stem: Two plants heterozygous for flower colour (Pp) are crossed. P (purple) is completely dominant to p (white). What phenotype ratio is expected?
options: 1 purple : 1 white
All purple
3 purple : 1 white
1 purple : 2 pink : 1 white
questions.explanation: The cross gives 1 PP : 2 Pp : 1 pp. PP and Pp both look purple because P is dominant, so the phenotypes are 3 purple : 1 white. A 1:2:1 phenotype ratio would only appear with incomplete dominance or codominance.

questions.stem: What is a test cross used to find out?
options: Whether an allele is dominant or recessive, by crossing two heterozygous parents
Which of two parents passed on a particular recessive allele to their offspring
Whether a trait is caused by a gene or by the environment the organism lives in
Whether an individual with the dominant phenotype is homozygous or heterozygous
questions.explanation: An individual with the dominant phenotype could be AA or Aa, so it is crossed with a homozygous recessive (aa). If any offspring show the recessive phenotype, the parent must be Aa; if all show the dominant phenotype in a large sample, it is most likely AA.

questions.stem: A black guinea pig is crossed with a white guinea pig (bb). Of 10 offspring, 6 are black and 4 are white. What is the black parent's genotype?
options: bb, because the other parent is white
Bb, because some offspring are white
BB, because most offspring are black
BB, because the ratio is not exactly 1:1
questions.explanation: Each white offspring is bb, so it received a b allele from the black parent, which must therefore be Bb. The expected ratio is 1:1, and 6:4 is a normal chance deviation in a small sample. A bb parent would be white, not black.

questions.stem: Two plants heterozygous for two genes that assort independently (AaBb × AaBb) are crossed, with A and B dominant. What phenotype ratio is expected?
questions.explanation: Each gene alone gives 3 dominant : 1 recessive, and independent genes combine by multiplying: 9 show both dominant traits, 3 and 3 show one of each, and 1 shows both recessive traits. A 1:1:1:1 ratio comes from crossing AaBb with aabb.

questions.stem: A plant heterozygous for two independently assorting genes (AaBb) is crossed with an aabb plant. What proportion of the offspring are expected to show both recessive traits?
questions.explanation: The AaBb parent makes four gamete types, AB, Ab, aB and ab, in equal proportions, and the aabb parent makes only ab. Offspring from the ab gamete are aabb, so 1/4 show both recessive traits. 1/16 is the answer for an AaBb × AaBb cross.

questions.stem: Why do linked genes not assort independently?
options: They code for the same protein, so they are inherited together as one single allele
They are carried on the sex chromosomes, which do not take part in meiosis
They are close together on the same chromosome, so they tend to be inherited together
They are on different chromosomes, which always move to the same pole in meiosis
questions.explanation: Independent assortment applies to genes on different chromosomes. Genes near each other on one chromosome travel together into gametes unless crossing over separates them, so their alleles are inherited as a unit more often than chance would predict.

questions.stem: Two genes are so close together on the same chromosome that crossing over between them almost never happens. A fly with alleles GL on one chromosome and gl on its homologue is crossed with a gl/gl fly. What offspring are expected?
options: Equal numbers of all four combinations: GL, Gl, gL and gl
A 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 ratio of the four possible phenotypes
A 3 : 1 ratio of dominant to recessive phenotypes
About half GL/gl and half gl/gl, the parental combinations only
questions.explanation: With no crossing over, the heterozygous parent only makes GL and gl gametes, so the offspring are half GL/gl and half gl/gl. Four equal classes would appear only if the genes assorted independently.

questions.stem: A fly with linked alleles AB on one chromosome and ab on the other is crossed with an ab/ab fly. Of 1000 offspring, 430 are AB, 420 ab, 80 Ab and 70 aB. What explains the Ab and aB offspring?
options: Crossing over between the two loci in the heterozygous parent during meiosis
Independent assortment of the two genes in the heterozygous parent
Crossing over between the two loci in the homozygous recessive parent
Mutation of the A gene in the gametes of the ab/ab parent
questions.explanation: Most offspring have the parental combinations, which shows the genes are linked; the few recombinants come from crossing over between the loci in the heterozygous parent. Independent assortment would give four roughly equal classes. Crossing over in an ab/ab parent produces only ab gametes, so it cannot create new combinations.

questions.stem: A test cross of a fly heterozygous for two linked genes gives 1000 offspring: 850 with the parental combinations and 150 recombinants. What is the recombination frequency between the genes?
questions.explanation: Recombination frequency is the number of recombinants divided by the total number of offspring, × 100: 150 ÷ 1000 × 100 = 15%. 85% is the proportion of parental types, and 17.6% wrongly divides by the parental total of 850 instead of all 1000 offspring.
